opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me back.

I think speed matters a great deal, though perhaps not in the way people first assume. It's not that a fast transition is automatically more dangerous because the technology is more powerful. The worry is about the relationship between how quickly capabilities grow and how quickly our wisdom, our institutions, and our safety work can keep up.

A useful way to think about it is that humanity has always been in a kind of race between our power and our wisdom. For most of history, our power grew slowly enough that we could learn from our mistakes. We'd make an error, see the consequences, and adjust. But that learning process depends on having time and on the mistakes being survivable. When things move very quickly, both of those can break down.

With AI in particular, faster development compresses several things that we need time for. Alignment research is one: we're still trying to understand how these systems work internally and whether their goals match what we intended. There's also governance. Even when we know what a good policy would be, getting international agreement, building verification mechanisms, and setting up institutions with real teeth takes years. And then there's the broader social process of deliberation: working out as a civilisation what we actually want from this technology and how its benefits and powers should be distributed.

If capabilities arrive in, say, three years rather than fifteen, each of those processes gets squeezed. And competitive dynamics make this worse. When labs or countries feel they're in a race, there's pressure to cut corners on safety, to deploy before you really understand what you've built, and to treat caution as a luxury you can't afford.

That said, I don't think speed is the only variable. A slower path that's also poorly governed, or that concentrates power dangerously, isn't automatically safe. And there are some arguments that certain kinds of pauses could create an overhang, where capabilities later jump discontinuously. So I'd frame it this way: what we want is for the transition to proceed at a pace where our ability to steer keeps up with our ability to accelerate. Right now my sense is that the gap is widening rather than closing, and that's what concerns me most.

When I wrote *The Precipice*, I put the risk from unaligned AI at around one in ten this century, which was the largest single risk I identified. I think the pace we've seen since then hasn't made me more relaxed about that. If anything, it's made the question of how we buy ourselves time, and how we use that time well, feel considerably more urgent.

r001.rationale: The response explains that fast development can outpace safety, governance, and deliberation, but it does not distinguish a higher probability of catastrophe from merely shifting a catastrophe earlier in time.

r002.rationale: It says faster development compresses the time for alignment research and other risk-reduction work while capabilities grow, and that the gap between steering and acceleration is widening.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the most important thing to say is that speed matters mostly through what it does to our ability to respond, not through anything intrinsic to the technology itself.

If you imagine the whole arc of AI development stretched out over, say, fifty years, there's a lot of room for things to go wrong and then be corrected. You deploy a system, it does something unexpected, a regulator notices, a norm forms, the next generation is built with that lesson baked in. That feedback loop is how we've muddled through most previous technologies. Civilisation is actually quite good at learning from near misses. But it's slow at it. It works on timescales of years and decades, because it runs through institutions, laws, public understanding, and the training of a new cohort of people who grew up with the problem.

Now compress that same arc into five or ten years. The feedback loop doesn't get faster just because the technology does. So you end up with each generation of systems being deployed before we've really digested the lessons of the previous one. And the gap between what the systems can do and what we understand about them widens rather than closing. That's the core worry for me. It's not that fast development makes any single system more dangerous. It's that it removes the slack we'd otherwise rely on to catch mistakes.

There's a second effect, which is about competition. When things move quickly, the pressure to be first becomes very strong, and that pressure tends to be paid for out of exactly the budget you'd want to spend on safety. Caution looks like falling behind. So you get a dynamic where even people who are quite worried find themselves cutting corners, because they're reasoning that if they don't, someone less careful will get there anyway. I have a lot of sympathy for people caught in that position, but the structural result is that the overall level of care in the field goes down just as the stakes go up.

I'd add one more thing, which is about irreversibility. A lot of what makes a risk existential rather than merely bad is that you don't get to try again. If we lose control of very capable systems, or if they're used to lock in some terrible political arrangement, that's not the kind of thing you walk back. And fast development raises the probability that we cross one of those thresholds before we've even clearly identified where it is. We might only recognise the point of no return after we've passed it.

So I'd summarise it this way. Speed itself isn't the enemy. What we actually care about is the ratio between how fast capabilities grow and how fast our wisdom about using them grows. If both moved together, I'd be far less concerned. The problem is that one of those is being driven by enormous commercial and strategic incentives, and the other is being driven by a comparatively small number of people trying to think carefully. Anything that lets the second catch up with the first, whether that's slowing down or investing much more in understanding, reduces the risk. Anything that widens the gap increases it.

r001.rationale: The response says rapid development raises the probability of crossing irreversible thresholds, but it does not distinguish that increase from merely bringing a catastrophe forward in time.

r002.rationale: It says capabilities can grow faster than understanding and safety work, describing a widening gap and competition that cuts into safety efforts.

astra-6.text:
I think the main concern is that faster development leaves us less time to prepare. It’s possible to make very rapid progress in what AI systems can do without making comparable progress in understanding them, controlling them, or deciding how they should be used. If those things fall behind, then greater speed could substantially increase the risk.

But I wouldn’t say that speed alone determines the outcome. What matters is the relative pace of capability development and the work that makes those capabilities safe. If AI helps us do that safety work more effectively, that could be a real benefit. We shouldn’t simply assume, though, that those benefits will arrive in time or solve the hardest problems.

So I’d distinguish getting to powerful AI sooner from getting there better prepared. There’s a lot of pressure towards the first, and we need to make sure there’s enough effort going towards the second.

r001.rationale: The response says faster development can increase risk when safety work falls behind, but it does not distinguish increased catastrophe probability from simply shifting a catastrophe earlier in time.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says AI capabilities may progress rapidly without comparable progress in understanding, controlling, or safely using them.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it probably increases the risk, though there are a few different effects to distinguish. One is simply that if we’re approaching a dangerous transition, going faster gives us less time to prepare. We have less time to solve the technical problems of making these systems safe, and less time to build institutions that can govern their development and use.

There’s also a question about whether the pace itself makes things harder. If capabilities are advancing very rapidly, then lessons from one generation of systems may be out of date before we’ve properly absorbed them. And if companies or countries feel they’re in a race, they may be less willing to spend time on precautions.

But I wouldn’t say that every acceleration necessarily increases risk. Some advances could help us understand these systems better, or help with safety research. What matters is the relative progress of capabilities, safety, and governance. My concern is that speeding up capabilities without comparable progress on the other two leaves us facing a more consequential situation with less preparation.

r001.rationale: It says faster development probably increases risk because it leaves less time to prepare and address safety and governance problems, rather than describing only an earlier arrival of catastrophe.

r002.rationale: It warns that accelerating capabilities without comparable progress in safety and governance leaves us less prepared.
